subtopics.title: Observation and scientific questions
subtopics.teaching: An observation records what is detected with senses or instruments; an inference explains what the observation may mean.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: a metal strip becomes longer when heated. Observation: its length increased. Inference: heating caused expansion.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not treat an explanation as an observation.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: separate observations, inferences and testable questions in an unfamiliar investigation.

subtopics.title: Variables and fair tests
subtopics.teaching: An independent variable is deliberately changed, the dependent variable is measured, and controlled variables are kept constant.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: to test how water temperature affects dissolving time, change temperature, measure time, and keep solute mass and water volume constant.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing several factors at once prevents a fair conclusion.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: design a fair test and identify independent, dependent and controlled variables.

subtopics.title: Measurement and units
subtopics.teaching: Choose an instrument and unit appropriate to the quantity: balance for mass, thermometer for temperature, ruler for length and stopwatch for time.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: record 25.0 cm rather than 25 cm when the instrument supports that precision.
subtopics.pitfall: Do not mix units such as centimetres and metres without conversion.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: select instruments, record suitable precision and convert units correctly.

subtopics.title: Tables graphs and evidence
subtopics.teaching: Tables organise measured values; graphs reveal patterns, trends and anomalies that may be harder to see in raw data.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: plot temperature on the horizontal axis and dissolving time on the vertical axis when temperature is the independent variable.
subtopics.pitfall: A graph scale must be read before comparing points.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: extract values, identify trends and use evidence without claiming more than the data shows.

subtopics.title: Claims explanations and conclusions
subtopics.teaching: A scientific claim should be supported by evidence and connected to reasoning that explains why the evidence supports it.
subtopics.worked_example: Example: if repeated trials show faster dissolving at higher temperatures, a cautious conclusion is that temperature affected dissolving rate under those conditions.
subtopics.pitfall: One unusual result should be examined rather than automatically discarded.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: write evidence-based conclusions and distinguish supported claims from speculation.

subtopics.title: States and properties of matter
subtopics.teaching: Matter has mass and occupies space. Solids keep a definite shape, liquids keep a definite volume but take the container's shape, and gases spread to fill their container.
subtopics.worked_example: A 100 mL liquid transferred to a different shaped vessel still occupies about the same volume.
subtopics.pitfall: A gas is not weightless simply because it is invisible.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: compare states using shape, volume, compressibility and particle arrangement.

subtopics.title: Physical and chemical changes
subtopics.teaching: A physical change alters form or state without creating a new substance; a chemical change produces new substances with different properties.
subtopics.worked_example: Melting ice is physical because water remains H2O; rusting iron is chemical because new iron oxides form.
subtopics.pitfall: Bubbles alone do not prove a chemical reaction because boiling also produces bubbles.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: classify unfamiliar changes and justify the classification using evidence.

subtopics.title: Mixtures and separation
subtopics.teaching: A mixture contains substances that retain their identities and can often be separated using physical properties such as particle size, solubility or boiling point.
subtopics.worked_example: Sand can be removed from water by filtration; dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporation.
subtopics.pitfall: Filtration cannot remove salt that is dissolved in water.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: choose and justify a separation method from the properties of the mixture.

subtopics.title: Materials and their uses
subtopics.teaching: Materials are selected for properties suited to a purpose: copper conducts electricity well, glass is transparent, rubber is flexible and waterproof.
subtopics.worked_example: Copper is useful in electrical wires because it combines high conductivity with workable ductility.
subtopics.pitfall: The strongest material is not automatically the best material for every application.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: match material properties to practical uses and explain trade-offs.

subtopics.title: Particle model reasoning
subtopics.teaching: The particle model explains macroscopic behaviour by considering how particles are arranged and move. Heating generally increases particle kinetic energy.
subtopics.worked_example: When a solid is heated, particles vibrate more strongly and may eventually overcome attractions enough for melting.
subtopics.pitfall: Particles do not become larger when a substance is heated; their motion changes.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: use particle reasoning to explain changes of state, diffusion and compression.

subtopics.title: Motion and speed
subtopics.teaching: Speed describes how much distance is covered per unit time: speed = distance ÷ time.
subtopics.worked_example: A cyclist travelling 120 m in 20 s has an average speed of 6 m/s.
subtopics.pitfall: A larger distance does not mean a greater speed unless the time interval is considered.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: calculate, compare and interpret speeds with correct units.

subtopics.title: Forces and interactions
subtopics.teaching: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's motion or shape. Forces occur through interactions between objects.
subtopics.worked_example: A book resting on a table experiences gravity downward and a support force upward.
subtopics.pitfall: An object moving at constant velocity can still have forces acting on it if they balance.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: identify interacting objects and the direction of forces in simple systems.

subtopics.title: Friction and resistance
subtopics.teaching: Friction and fluid resistance oppose relative motion. They can be useful, such as providing grip, or unwanted, such as causing energy loss.
subtopics.worked_example: Tyre tread increases grip by improving interaction with the road; lubricants reduce friction between moving surfaces.
subtopics.pitfall: Removing all friction is not always desirable because walking and braking depend on friction.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: predict how changing surfaces or conditions affects motion.

subtopics.title: Heat and temperature
subtopics.teaching: Temperature indicates how hot or cold a system is, while thermal energy concerns the internal energy associated with particle motion and interactions.
subtopics.worked_example: A metal spoon and a cup of hot water can have different temperatures and different amounts of thermal energy because their masses differ.
subtopics.pitfall: Temperature and heat are not interchangeable terms.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: distinguish temperature from thermal energy and predict heating or cooling changes.

subtopics.title: Light and reflection
subtopics.teaching: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium and can be reflected when it meets a surface.
subtopics.worked_example: A plane mirror forms an image with the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence.
subtopics.pitfall: The reflected ray is not automatically perpendicular to the mirror.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: trace rays and apply the law of reflection to unfamiliar diagrams.

subtopics.title: Sound and vibration
subtopics.teaching: Sound is produced by vibrating sources and travels through a material medium as a mechanical wave.
subtopics.worked_example: A vibrating ruler overhanging a table produces sound because its vibration disturbs the surrounding air.
subtopics.pitfall: Sound cannot propagate through a vacuum because there is no material medium.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: connect frequency and vibration to pitch and explain why sound needs a medium.

subtopics.title: Ecosystems and food webs
subtopics.teaching: An ecosystem includes organisms interacting with each other and with their physical environment. Food webs show interconnected feeding relationships and energy transfer.
subtopics.worked_example: If a predator population falls, prey numbers may rise and affect organisms at other trophic levels.
subtopics.pitfall: A food web is not a simple list because one organism can have several feeding relationships.
subtopics.mastery: Mastery: predict population changes from disruptions to a food web.
